contacts.subject: Testing turns at field boundaries
contacts.body:
Hi Nic,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The recovery side of my work has made me interested in plans that work until there isn't quite enough room to carry them out. I was reading about Agtonomy's multi-point turns and wondering how small changes in the available turning space affect whether the machine can finish the manoeuvre.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project around testing those limits alongside my current work. One idea would be to build a set of simulated turning scenarios and search for the layouts where a plan needs to change, though I'd rather work on a problem the team already needs help with. Would that kind of testing be useful?

Happy to send my resume over, and happy to talk if it sounds worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: When forecast errors change the decision
contacts.body:
Hi Sean,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The simulation side of my work has made me interested in the difference between a prediction being wrong and it being wrong enough to change what you should do. With Amperon's probabilistic solar and wind forecasts, I'd be curious which forecast errors actually change a battery's charging plan.

I'd be interested in a small contract project building a backtest around that question. One idea would be to compare battery schedules made from successive forecasts and see where the extra information changes the decision or its cost. Would that be useful to the team, or is there another forecast-evaluation problem you'd rather have someone take on?

Happy to send my resume over, and happy to talk if it sounds worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Chinmay,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

A lot of the planning work I do is about recovering a useful plan after one action becomes impossible. With TerraMax working under canopy and on uneven ground, I'd be curious how much of a field plan needs to change when a route to the next area can no longer be used.

Andrew

contacts.subject: Replanning when a pickup takes longer
contacts.body:
Hi Kristoffer,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The recovery work has made me interested in how much of a schedule should change after one job takes longer than expected. With Spare's live paratransit routing, I'd be curious when recovering a delayed pickup is worth changing the plan for passengers who were still on time.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project around that tradeoff. One idea would be to simulate longer boarding times and compare how replanning strategies recover lateness without creating as much disruption elsewhere. Would that be useful to the team, or is there another routing problem you'd rather have someone work on?

Happy to send my resume over, and happy to talk if it sounds worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Nathan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I emailed Paul earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since you're closer to the ML side at Aclima. Reading about the mobile mapping work, I got interested in the route-planning problem; with limited driving time, where you send the cars changes what you get to observe and what you miss.

Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my planning and ML work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on for that kind of real-world impact. One idea would be to simulate different routing strategies under the same driving budget and test whether smarter route selection improves the resulting map, but I'd rather shape it around whatever planning problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

Hi Vibhor,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

Burro seemed like a good fit because an outdoor robot needs to handle changing surroundings without someone constantly getting it unstuck. That connection between navigation and recovery is close to what I’ve been working on.

One thought was a simulation and evaluation harness around navigation recovery, testing what happens when a path becomes blocked or the robot is uncertain about its position, but I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to the team.

Best,
Andrew

submitted.subject: UofT student hoping to make outdoor robots more useful
submitted.body:
Hi Vibhor,

I’m a UofT student currently on co-op in London working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around finding failures and recovery paths in large systems. I’ve also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’m looking for work where the systems I build make something physically easier for people, and Burro seemed like a good fit because an outdoor robot needs to handle changing surroundings without someone constantly getting it unstuck. That connection between navigation and recovery is close to what I’ve been working on.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. One thought was a simulation and evaluation harness around navigation recovery, testing what happens when a path becomes blocked or the robot is uncertain about its position, but I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to the team.

I attached my resume for context; happy to jump on a quick call if there might be something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

Hi James,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The biotech work has also made me interested in how you choose the next experiment, which is what drew me to Citrine’s materials work. When you only have a few measurements and each test takes time and uses material, the uncertainty should affect what you decide to try next.

I was wondering if there might be a project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. One thought was a benchmark comparing experiment-selection strategies under limited observations, measurement uncertainty and a fixed test budget, but I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to the research team.

My resume is attached for context.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Steve,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I sent James a note earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since this seemed close to your research engineering work. I was reading about Citrine's materials work and got interested in the experiment-selection problem; when you can only run so many tests, each result changes what looks worth trying next.

Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my planning and ML work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare experiment-selection strategies under the same test budget and see which ones reach a useful candidate faster, but I'd rather shape it around whatever question would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Martha,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’d like to do more work on finding where a model stops being reliable, which is what drew me to Development Seed’s geospatial work. I was thinking about models that work well on one set of imagery but behave differently when the region, sensor or available coverage changes.

I was wondering if there might be a project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. One thought was evaluation tooling to test how a geospatial model behaves across regions and with missing imagery or changing sensor conditions, but I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to your team.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Sajjad,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed Martha earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since you lead engineering at Development Seed. With land-cover mapping, I'd be interested in cases where a model reports a change on the ground just because the imagery came from a different sensor.

Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my ML work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare predictions for the same locations across different sensors and test where switching sensors changes the land-cover prediction, but I'd rather shape it around whatever evaluation problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed Martha earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too since you lead engineering at Development Seed. With land-cover mapping, I'd be interested in cases where a model reports a change on the ground just because the imagery came from a different sensor.

Lately I've been looking for ways to use more of my ML work on problems with a real-world benefit, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare predictions for the same locations across different sensors and test where switching sensors changes the land-cover prediction, but I'd rather shape it around whatever evaluation problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Lilly,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed Martha earlier today, but thought I'd ask you directly given your work with satellite imagery. I'd like to do more work on finding where a model stops being reliable. The question I'd want to test is whether a model trained on one set of imagery still gives sensible predictions when the same landscape is observed by a different sensor.

I'd be interested in taking on a small contract project building evaluation tooling around that, alongside my current work. I could use matched examples to separate changes in the imagery from actual changes on the ground, then look for cases where the model confuses the two. Is that something your team needs to test, or is there another evaluation problem that's more useful right now?

Happy to send my resume over.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

Hi Ed,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’d like to use the failure-analysis side of that work on problems where it can help keep infrastructure safe, which is why Gecko caught my attention. I’m interested in what you can reliably conclude from an inspection when some areas haven’t been covered, and how that changes where you should inspect next.

An offline evaluation of those gaps and their effect on anomaly detection seems like a project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. I’d be curious whether that would be useful, or if there’s a more pressing question around the inspection data that the team hasn’t had time to explore.

My resume is attached; happy to jump on a call if useful.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Fernando,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed David earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too given your work detecting vessels in satellite imagery. I was reading about Global Fishing Watch and got interested in what happens when the AIS history is incomplete and satellite imagery only catches a vessel intermittently; you’re trying to piece together what it was doing from observations that can leave pretty large gaps.

I've wanted to find a way to use more of my ML work on ocean conservation for a while, and this felt close enough to what I already do that I could be useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to test how gaps in vessel observations change the interpretation of a track or make its identity ambiguous, but I'd rather shape it around whatever problem would actually be useful to the research team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Charlie,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’ve been looking for a way to use that planning work to improve accessibility, and GoodMaps interested me because a route has to remain useful when someone’s position is uncertain or a section turns out not to be accessible. Working out how to recover from that is close to the problems I’ve been spending time on.

Could there be a project for me around testing those cases? I was thinking about simulating ambiguous positioning and blocked or inaccessible route segments, then comparing how a navigation system recovers. I’d be doing it alongside my current work and would rather start with whatever issue the team actually needs help with.

I attached my resume for context.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Brian,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The planning side of my work has made me interested in when a plan needs to change and when it is better left alone. With Overstory's vegetation work, I'd be curious how you decide whether new risk information is worth changing a crew's existing work plan.

contacts.subject: Evaluating imaging models across datasets
contacts.body:
Hi Preetham,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The evaluation work is something I’d like to do more of, particularly on medical tools where a model’s errors matter beyond a test score. With Qure, I’d be curious where changes in image quality or the source dataset start to affect a model’s results, even when it performs well on its original test data.

Is there an evaluation project around those differences I could take ownership of alongside my current work? I’d work with existing research data and whatever comparisons the AI team actually needs, rather than assume a particular model or dataset is the right starting point.

My resume is attached for context; happy to talk if useful.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

Hi Topher,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

One problem I’d like to spend more time on is figuring out why a model stops being reliable once the conditions change. I was wondering if there might be a small contract project around that kind of problem that I could take ownership of alongside my current work. I could help build evaluation tooling to isolate which changes in background sound are actually responsible for detections breaking across sites, though I’d much rather work from whatever question the team already needs answered.

I attached my resume for context. Happy to talk if there’s something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

before.body:
Hi Scott,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The recovery side of planning is something I’d like to do more of outside biotech, and Routific got me thinking about how much of a delivery plan really needs to change after a stop runs late or a new order comes in. I’d be interested in keeping the plan useful without adding unnecessary driving.

I was wondering whether there might be a project I could take ownership of around that. I could compare replanning approaches under delayed stops, changing travel times and new orders, including how much disruption each approach introduces to the existing plan. I’d be happy to start with a different optimization problem if that would be more useful to the team.

I’d be doing this alongside my current work. I attached my resume for context. Happy to talk if there’s something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

sent_messages.name: Scott Justason
sent_messages.last_sent_body:
Hi Scott,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

A lot of the planning work I’m doing now is about what to do once the original plan stops being valid, and I’d like to do more of that outside biotech. Routific seemed interesting for that reason. If one delivery runs late, there’s a tradeoff between replanning enough to recover the schedule and changing so much that you create new problems elsewhere.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project on that kind of recovery problem that I could take ownership of alongside my current work. One possible starting point would be to simulate delays and compare different replanning strategies by how much lateness they recover and how much of the original route they disrupt. But I’d rather work from a problem the team already cares about than force that exact idea.

I attached my resume for context. Happy to talk if there’s something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Kevin,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed Scott earlier today, but thought I'd ask you directly given your operations research work. A lot of the planning work I'm doing is about recovering once the original plan stops being valid. If one delivery runs late, I'd be interested in how much of the route needs to change to recover the schedule without disrupting everything else.

I'd be interested in taking ownership of a small contract project comparing replanning strategies alongside my current work. I could simulate delays and compare how much lateness each strategy recovers against how much of the existing plan it changes. Is that a problem the team is working on, or is there another routing question you'd rather have someone take on?

Happy to send my resume over.

Best,
Andrew

My resume is attached for context; happy to talk if there might be something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

sent_messages.name: Laura Read
sent_messages.role: Director of Technical and Federal Partnerships, HydroForecast
sent_messages.last_sent_body:
Hi Laura,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’d like to do more simulation work around how uncertainty changes a decision, which is what drew me to HydroForecast. One case I’ve been thinking about is a forecast that gets the total amount of water roughly right but gets the timing of the peak wrong, and how much that changes the choices a reservoir operator can make.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. I could simulate reservoir decisions as an expected inflow peak arrives earlier or later than forecast and look at which decisions are most sensitive to that timing error, though I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to the team.

My resume is attached; happy to talk if there might be something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Joel,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. I’d much rather work from whatever problem the engineering team actually needs answered, though.

My resume is attached for context; happy to talk if there might be something useful I could take on.


Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Utility context for building investigations
contacts.body:
Hi Carl,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The business dashboard already lets teams investigate air-quality readings and configure building alerts. I wondered whether a Canadian utility report could be useful context when a customer is checking a disconnected hub or changing conditions around HVAC equipment.

Do your business customers need that wider grid view when troubleshooting, or is the local sensor data usually enough?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: OutageHub for Alert Labs
contacts.body:
Hi Cliffton,

I wanted to make the question in my July note more concrete. Sensor Relay already reports power loss at the building. The possible addition from OutageHub is the utility’s wider outage report alongside that local event.

If several properties report power loss together, your team could check whether the utility is also reporting an outage around them.

Is that area-level context already available in AlertAQ, or would it be useful to look at it for one Canadian property group?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko

contacts.subject: Outage context in Risk Intelligence
contacts.body:
Hi Ben,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

AlertMedia already connects threats to the people and assets that may be affected. I thought utility outage reports could be useful in that same workflow: a customer could see which Canadian locations overlap a reported outage, then decide whether anyone there needs an update.

Is that already covered by your current data sources, or would it be useful to look at the feed?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Pete Dombrowski
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: An outage feed for ThreatWatcher
contacts.body:
Hi Pete,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ThreatWatcher already turns location-specific weather warnings, including Environment Canada alerts, into notifications. I wondered whether utility outage reports could use a similar path, giving customers reported grid conditions around their sites alongside the weather warnings.

Is that a feed your product team would find useful, or is it already covered?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: When a charging site goes offline
contacts.body:
Hi Jonas,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Ampcontrol already brings charger monitoring, notifications and support into one workflow. A Canadian utility outage feed could give your team another piece of context when a whole charging site goes offline, before they work through charger-level troubleshooting.

Would that be useful for the Canadian sites your customers operate?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context for charging sites
contacts.body:
Hi Alexander,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

AMPECO already exposes charging-management functions through its APIs. That looks like a possible place for Canadian utility reports: when a site becomes unavailable, the operator could see whether an outage is also being reported around it before working through charger-level checks.

Is that already part of the context available to your Canadian operators?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context when monitoring goes offline
contacts.body:
Hi Tal,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Atera’s device monitoring depends on an online agent that can reach the network. When a Canadian customer site loses that visibility, a utility report could give the MSP some external context alongside the alerts and tickets it is already reviewing.

Would that be useful for the site-level incident workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for offline sites
contacts.body:
Hi Valerie,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Auvik gives MSPs a view of network health across their customer sites. When several sites stop responding, I thought it could help to show whether their locations also overlap a reported utility outage. That would give technicians some external context alongside what they can see from the network itself.

Do you already bring Canadian outage reports into that view?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context in weather layers
contacts.body:
Hi Tony,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Baron’s ArcGIS-ready layers let teams inspect weather hazards alongside their assets. A Canadian utility feed could sit beside those layers, so a customer investigating an event can also see where power disruption is being reported.

contacts.subject: Grid context around monitored workers
contacts.body:
Hi Mike,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Blackline Connect already exposes device locations and safety alerts. I wondered whether Canadian utility reports could provide useful surrounding context for the monitoring team, particularly when they need to understand conditions around several workers or facilities during an incident.

Would an area-level outage report help that workflow, or would it add little beyond the signals you already have?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for ARIA
contacts.body:
Hi Omar,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ARIA already uses building data to help teams investigate HVAC issues. I thought Canadian utility reports could add context outside the building, so a facilities team reviewing an interruption can see whether a wider outage is being reported nearby.

Is that information already available to ARIA when it helps with a building issue?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Hi Mike,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Asset Essentials already receives connected-asset measurements through Smart Assets. I wondered whether a Canadian utility report could sit alongside a site-related maintenance issue, giving the team some wider context before assigning separate equipment investigations.

Would that be useful at the point where asset alerts become maintenance work?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outages in CARTO Workflows
contacts.body:
Hi Vanessa,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Your flood-claims workflow shows how an external event feed can be matched against properties in CARTO. I thought Canadian utility outages could support a similar use case, letting customers see which of their assets sit inside a reported outage area using the spatial tools they already have.

Would this be worth exploring as a data partnership?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Would that be useful in the way customers investigate a shared site interruption?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage data alongside charger status
contacts.body:
Hi Kelvin,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ChargeLab's API already gives operators access to their stations and charger status. I thought an outage feed could sit alongside that information, so a support team can check whether an offline Canadian charging site overlaps a utility-reported outage before investigating individual chargers.

Would that add useful context to the monitoring workflow, or is it something you already cover?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context in charger management
contacts.body:
Hi Razvan,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ChargePoint already gives operators station reports through its management portal. When a Canadian charging site becomes unavailable, a utility report could give the person investigating it some area context alongside the station data.

Is there a place for that in the charger-management workflow you work on?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in RMM alert correlation
contacts.body:
Hi Johannes,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ConnectWise RMM already correlates related alerts across the infrastructure an MSP monitors. I thought Canadian utility reports could add an external input to a site investigation, so the technician can check for a reported area outage alongside the device alerts.

Does RMM already provide that Canadian grid context to partners?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in ProAct alarms
contacts.body:
Hi Niels,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ProAct already brings refrigeration and HVAC alarms to a remote monitoring team. I thought Canadian utility reports could sit alongside those alarms, helping the team check whether several sites are near a reported grid interruption before narrowing the investigation to individual equipment.

Is that Canadian utility-level context already available in the workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.body:
Hi Brittany,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Kaizen already helps building teams find faults across their equipment and building systems. I wondered whether that could fit alongside the building data you already bring into Kaizen.

Do your Canadian customers need that wider grid view when reviewing alarms?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage context in Horizon
contacts.body:
Hi Cathy,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Horizon already brings risk events, customer locations and communications together. Canadian utility reports could provide another event layer for that workflow, helping an operations team identify sites near a reported outage and decide where to check in.

Would it be useful to compare our feed with how Horizon handles Canadian power disruptions today?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage reports in D4H incident maps
contacts.body:
Hi Robin,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

D4H Incident Management already puts maps, weather and status boards in front of response teams. I thought a Canadian outage layer could give those teams a clearer view of reported power disruption around facilities during an incident, without making them check separate utility maps.

Is there a place for that in the incident-management workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Hi Michael,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The Dataminr and Esri integration already places event intelligence alongside the assets a team is protecting. I thought utility-reported outages could be useful supporting context for Canadian locations, especially when an emerging incident may involve a wider power disruption.

Would your integrations team have a use for a feed like this, or is it already covered?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility reports in enteliWEB
contacts.body:
Hi Will,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

enteliWEB already manages multiple sites and can bring in alarms from non-BACnet systems. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit alongside those inputs, helping operators check for an area outage when several building systems raise alarms together.

Is external utility information something the product already brings into that view?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context through ECLYPSE
contacts.body:
Hi Charles,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ECLYPSE’s REST API lets developers connect controller data with building applications. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful alongside that data, giving the team reviewing building faults some context outside the property itself.

Would that fit the integrations your product team wants developers to build?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context for Domotz sites
contacts.body:
Hi Andrea,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Domotz already organizes monitored devices around customer sites and lets teams extend their dashboards through the API. That looks like a natural place to add Canadian utility outage context: when a site drops offline, a technician could check whether the surrounding area has a reported outage before narrowing the problem to individual devices.

Would it be useful to look at this for the MSP workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in Network Optimizer
contacts.body:
Hi Oren,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Network Optimizer already brings monitoring, incident handling and remediation together. I thought Canadian outage reports could help the operator reviewing an incident understand whether it coincides with a wider grid event, alongside what the chargers themselves are reporting.

Is external outage data already part of that workflow for your Canadian networks?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Power disruption as a portfolio layer
contacts.body:
Hi Sarah,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Ascend already combines environmental hazards and partner datasets around asset portfolios. I wondered whether reported power disruptions could add useful context for Canadian properties, particularly when analysts are trying to understand the effects of a wider environmental event.

Would live outage information be useful to those users, or is the more relevant question historical reliability?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Daniel Flanigan
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: Utility context for interval alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Daniel,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

UtilityManagement already connects buildings, meters and interval-data alerts. When a team investigates an unusual or missing interval at a Canadian site, a utility outage report could provide context without assuming the meter itself has failed.

Would your users have a use for that connection in an interval-data investigation?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage feed for asset maps
contacts.body:
Hi Erica,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ArcGIS Velocity already lets customers combine live data with asset locations and trigger alerts from spatial analysis. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit that workflow, giving a team a way to identify assets inside a reported outage area and bring that information into its operational dashboard.

Would it be worth looking at how this could reach your Canadian customers?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context in EV Connect
contacts.body:
Hi Nicholas,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Your API platform lets operators build around the charging sites they manage. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit alongside site status, so support teams can check for a reported grid interruption while investigating unavailable chargers.

Do Canadian operators already have that wider utility view in their workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.body:
Hi Mathew,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Visual Command Center already combines external risk feeds with customer assets and communications. I thought Canadian utility reports could add detail to that view during a power disruption, so an operator can compare the reported outage area with the locations they are responsible for.

How is that Canadian utility-level context handled in VCC today?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility events near supply-chain sites
contacts.body:
Hi Alejandro,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Everstream already monitors disruptive events that could affect supply-chain operations. Canadian utility reports could give the analyst another location-based input, helping identify supplier or logistics sites that warrant a local status check during a reported outage.

Is that utility-level information already covered by your data products?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for building faults
contacts.body:
Hi Raj,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Facilio brings building operations together across a portfolio. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful when several systems at a site stop responding: the facilities team could check for a reported area outage alongside the building data it is already reviewing.

Is that external utility context part of the workflow your customers use?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outages and True Impact
contacts.body:
Hi Greta,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

True Impact already connects verified incidents with the locations a customer cares about. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful alongside those incidents, helping a team see whether a reported power disruption overlaps its offices or other assets.

Is that a data source your team would want to evaluate for this workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context in building work orders
contacts.body:
Hi Stuart,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The Switch Automation integration can turn building conditions and custom alerts into Fiix work orders. I thought a Canadian utility report could be attached at that point, helping the person triaging the work check for an area outage before treating each alarm as a separate equipment issue.

Is there a place for that kind of external context in the integration?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.body:
Hi Antoine,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

FLO's network operations center already monitors charging stations and helps coordinate repairs. When a Canadian site becomes unavailable, I thought a utility outage report could give the NOC useful context before it decides what needs further investigation or a service visit.

Does the team already have a consistent way to check that across utilities?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for fleet charging sites
contacts.body:
Hi Foued,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Foresta already combines real-time charging monitoring with a platform integrators can build around. I thought Canadian utility reports could sit beside site status, giving fleet support teams some wider context when a charging location becomes unavailable.

Do your operators already have a consistent utility feed for that check?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context in the Fusion Framework
contacts.body:
Hi Steve,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Fusion already connects weather alerts and asset impact with its response workflows. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit alongside those events, so teams can see which sites overlap a reported outage before assessing the effects on their operations.

Would it be useful to look at the feed for that workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko

contacts.subject: Utility context for charging integrations
contacts.body:
Hi Radu,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

I wrote to Mike earlier this summer about Canadian outage data. Your charging integrations make the use case more specific: a fleet team already seeing vehicle and charging-station information could also check whether a depot is near a reported utility outage when charging becomes unavailable.

Is that something the platform product team already handles through a data partner?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context in GEM alarms
contacts.body:
Hi Daniel,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

GEM already gives operators cooler, freezer and other site-equipment alarms. If several alarms arrive during a reported Canadian utility outage, showing that report alongside them could help the facilities team decide which local checks to make first.

Do operators already have that wider utility context in GEM?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko

Hi Alex,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Houski already supplies Canadian property data and climate-risk information through its API. I wondered whether your users also need to understand past utility interruptions around a property, as another reliability input beside the location data you already provide.

Is outage history something your customers ask about?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Jorge Pantoja
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: Outage context in JPlug
contacts.body:
Hi Jorge,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

JPlug already gives operators charging monitoring and APIs for their own applications. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit alongside charger status, so an operator can check for an area outage when a whole site stops responding.

Would that be useful for the sites your platform manages?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid events alongside building alarms
contacts.body:
Hi Ard,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

KODE OS already brings building systems and fault rules together across a portfolio. If several systems stop reporting at once, Canadian utility outage information could give the operations team some context outside the building before they work through individual alarms.

Would that fit how your customers investigate incidents in KODE OS?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Gabriel Damant-Sirois
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: Outage history in property data
contacts.body:
Hi Gabriel,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Local Logic already gives property products Canadian location data and climate-risk context. I wondered whether those users also ask about past utility interruptions around a property, as a separate reliability question alongside the risks you already describe.

Would outage history be useful in that workflow, or does it sit outside what your customers need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context for IoT work orders
contacts.body:
Hi Marcel,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

MaintainX already connects live sensor data with maintenance work. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful context for a site-related event, so technicians can check whether a wider outage is being reported while they assess the equipment itself.

Would an input like that fit the IoT partnerships you work on?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage layers for site maps
contacts.body:
Hi Dietmar,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Mapbox already gives developers location data and tools for joining information to geographic areas. I thought a Canadian outage layer could be useful for applications that display customer facilities, letting users inspect utility reports beside the sites on their map.

Is that the kind of operational dataset your data-services team would consider?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Luca Humbel

contacts.subject: Canadian outage data beside weather
contacts.body:
Hi Luca,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Your Weather API brings several datasets into a common interface, including coverage in Canada. I wondered whether utility outage reports could be useful to customers building operational tools, as another input they can inspect alongside weather conditions.

Do those customers ask for observed grid-disruption data, or is that usually handled elsewhere?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in disconnected-site alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Simon,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Monta’s alerting already flags disconnected charge points and faults for operators. With the Canadian launch, I thought utility reports could be useful alongside those alerts, helping support teams check for a reported area outage when several chargers at a site become unavailable.

Is that wider grid context already part of the Canadian operator workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context for building incidents
contacts.body:
Hi Joshua,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

MRI's IoT Hub already takes in building-system alarms and can turn them into actions. I thought there might be a useful connection with external utility reports, so a facilities team reviewing alarms at a Canadian site can also see whether there is a reported outage nearby.

Would this be worth discussing with the team that owns the building-alarm integrations?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in Mysa HQ
contacts.body:
Hi Joey,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Mysa HQ already brings HVAC and refrigeration monitoring together with email and SMS alerts. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful when several systems at a location need attention, giving the facilities team a wider reference before it starts arranging equipment checks.

Do your multi-site customers already have that grid context alongside the alerts?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Greg Thomas
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: Grid context when a delegate goes offline
contacts.body:
Hi Greg,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Your NMS documentation describes how a site’s monitoring depends on its delegate being online. If that delegate stops responding, a Canadian utility report could give the technician an external reference while local polling is unavailable.

Is that information already brought into the site investigation in NinjaOne?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context on Noggin maps
contacts.body:
Hi Simon,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Noggin already maps assets against events and connects that view to incident notifications. Canadian utility reports could sit alongside those events, helping response teams see which facilities are near a reported outage and decide where they need a local update.

Would this add anything to the way your Canadian customers use Noggin today?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for OptigoVN sites
contacts.body:
Hi Pook-Ping,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

OptigoVN already gives facilities teams a view of their building networks across a campus. When a building’s devices stop responding, a Canadian utility report could provide context outside the OT network while the team investigates the local cause.

Would that be useful alongside the site-level information in OptigoVN?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context for remote PRTG sites
contacts.body:
Hi Christoph,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

PRTG already helps teams monitor distributed branches and customer sites. When a site stops responding, Canadian utility reports could give the technician an external reference while they investigate, before narrowing the incident to individual devices.

Would that fit the technical integrations your team supports for MSPs?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage data alongside Weather Source
contacts.body:
Hi Shannon,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Weather Source already gives other products access to weather information through an API. I thought reported power disruptions could be a useful companion for Canadian operations teams that want to see what is happening on the grid alongside the weather conditions.

Is that the kind of additional dataset your B2B team would consider?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Hi Andy,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Data Graph now covers Canadian addresses, buildings and parcels alongside its other location-linked datasets. I thought reported utility outages could be another useful layer around those locations, for customers who need to understand current disruption as well as the characteristics of a property.

Would this fit the way you evaluate additional data products?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context in WhatsUp Gold
contacts.body:
Hi Derek,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The TTNA case shows WhatsUp Gold monitoring several facilities, including one in Ontario. I thought a utility report could sit beside that site view, giving the network team an external reference when a facility’s devices become unavailable together.

Would that fit the way WhatsUp Gold handles context for distributed-site incidents?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian detail in outage alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Erick,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Regroup already includes utility outages in its map-based threat monitoring. The question for us is whether normalized reports from Canadian utilities would add any useful geographic detail to those events, especially when a customer is checking several locations.

Does your existing source already provide the Canadian utility detail those customers need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Hi Archana,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.body:
Hi Claudia,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Riskline already reports outage-related travel disruption, including events in Canada. I wondered whether direct utility reports would add any useful geographic detail to that intelligence, particularly when a platform customer needs to understand conditions around a specific location.

Does your current coverage already provide the Canadian utility detail your analysts need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage data in FME
contacts.body:
Hi George,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Your real-time FME examples connect incoming data to GIS dashboards and email actions. I thought a Canadian outage feed could follow the same path: customers could join utility reports to their own facilities, then decide what belongs in a dashboard or notification.

Would that be worth looking at as a data integration for FME users?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility reports on the security map
contacts.body:
Hi Olof,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Safeture’s security overview already shows alerts, facilities and end-user locations together. Canadian utility reports could add context to that map, helping a risk team identify facilities that warrant a local status check during a reported outage.

Does the current intelligence already provide that Canadian utility detail?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Dan McEleney

contacts.subject: Utility reports alongside Samdesk alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Dan,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Samdesk already connects emerging events to facilities and other locations a customer monitors. I thought Canadian utility reports could add useful detail when an incident involves power disruption, so the customer can compare the reported outage area with the places it is responsible for.

Would it be useful to look at the feed alongside your current Canadian event coverage?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for fleet charging
contacts.body:
Hi David,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The PowerFlex integration connects Samsara fleet data with charger health and charging information. I thought Canadian utility reports could add another piece of context when a fleet team is investigating an unavailable depot charging site.

Would this belong with your charging partners, or does Samsara already provide that utility context?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Grid context for service-provider incidents
contacts.body:
Hi Michael,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

SL1 already gives service providers a way to monitor their customers' devices. I thought Canadian utility reports could add an external view when several devices or sites stop responding, helping the operations team see whether the incident coincides with a wider grid event.

Would that be useful in the site and service incident workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Zachary Wolf
contacts.reason: First product/data owner to test the stated integration and identify an evaluation sponsor.
contacts.subject: Outage context before a service visit
contacts.body:
Hi Zachary,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

ServiceChannel already connects asset alarms to work orders and service providers. I thought a Canadian outage check could be useful at that decision point, giving the facilities team more context before treating an unavailable asset as an equipment problem that needs a visit.

Is external utility information something you already bring into that workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage events in Signal4D
contacts.body:
Hi David,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Signal4D already gives developers weather alerts from sources including Environment Canada. I thought utility reports could be a useful companion for applications monitoring customer locations, showing reported grid disruption alongside the weather alerts.

Would that fit the event data your API customers need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Utility context in InformaCast
contacts.body:
Hi Cameron,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The incident-mapping work in InformaCast connects notifications to the place where an event is happening. I thought utility reports could add context for Canadian campuses, helping a response team see reported power disruption around its facilities and decide which groups need an update.

Would that fit the way your team evaluates inputs to InformaCast?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outage context in travel alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Adam,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Sitata already gives travel platforms destination risk data and alert notifications through developer integrations. I thought Canadian utility reports could add detail when a trip involves a location with reported power disruption, alongside the other local events you monitor.

Would that fit the disruption information your platform customers need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Is that external utility context already part of the multi-site monitoring workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

Hi Martin,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

StormGeo already sends weather alerts to people within customer organizations. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful alongside those alerts, so operations teams can also see where power disruption is being reported as conditions change.

Would that be relevant to the alerting products your team works on?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.name: Akhilesh Subramanian
contacts.reason: Selected product/data owner or practical technical champion for the documented workflow.
contacts.subject: Grid context for client-site alerts
contacts.body:
Hi Akhilesh,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

SuperOps already applies monitoring policies by client, site and asset, with alerts feeding into tickets. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful at the site level, helping an MSP check whether a wider outage is being reported before investigating each affected endpoint.

Is that an input your product team would consider for the monitoring workflow?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Outage context for building networks
contacts.body:
Hi Katie,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

The Oxford work with Switch Dx³ looks at connected systems and network health across Canadian buildings. I thought utility reports could add a useful external reference when a building’s devices stop responding, alongside the network information your platform already captures.

Is that context something your building operations users need?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: From weather alerts to outage context
contacts.body:
Hi Maya,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Tomorrow.io already brings government weather alerts into its platform and API. I thought utility reports could add a useful view of current disruption for Canadian locations, so operations teams can compare a weather event with where power outages are actually being reported.

Would that be a useful addition for the customers using your operational alerts?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Power context for Xweather Protect
contacts.body:
Hi Hans,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Xweather Protect already configures weather alerts around customer assets. I thought Canadian utility reports could fit alongside those alerts, giving an operator another view of reported disruption around a site as conditions change.

Do your customers have a use for that connection between weather hazards and power outages?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Canadian outages on monitoring maps
contacts.body:
Hi Samirs,

I’m Andrew, founder of OutageHub. We bring public power-outage reports from Canadian utilities into one API.

Zabbix already lets integrators configure geographic monitoring views through the dashboard API. I thought Canadian utility reports could be useful beside the monitored sites, helping a team check whether a group of host issues coincides with a reported area outage.

Is this the kind of data integration your Canadian partners would have a use for?

Thanks,
Andrew Gordienko
Founder, OutageHub

contacts.subject: Montréal-Est automation
contacts.body:
Hi Suresh,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the metal-processing operation at Montréal-Est. We’re looking for one metal-processing line where we can benchmark the time lost to human recovery and test software against the recurring cases. A measured result there would give us a basis for assessing whether the approach is useful elsewhere in the group.

Would you be the right person for a short call about a possible Montréal-Est pilot, or could you point me toward whoever owns the automation there?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Montréal-Est automation
contacts.body:
Hi Eric,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the metal-processing operation at Montréal-Est. We could start with one processing stage, quantify the productive time lost when people have to recover it, and test whether software can reduce that loss while preserving the required output quality.

Would you be the right person for a short call about this, or could you point me toward whoever owns the process?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Steeve,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The waterjet cutting work at the Sherbrooke plant caught my attention. If the cycle and fault records are available, we could use them to separate interrupted cuts from normal setup work, identify the recovery sequences taking the most time, and test whether software can shorten them without affecting part quality.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

The waterjet cutting work at the Sherbrooke plant caught my attention. A cutting-line pilot could measure productive time lost to interrupted cycles, identify which recoveries account for most of it, and test software against those cases while checking finished-part quality.

If those interruptions are affecting production, would you be open to a short call to work out whether a pilot would be useful?

Best,
Andrew

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

contacts.subject: Trois-Rivières automation
contacts.body:
Hi Yves,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I saw the July update on optical sorting and glass drying at Trois-Rivières. We could baseline the time spent recovering the sorting and drying stages, identify the interruptions that matter most to usable glass output, and test whether software can reduce that loss without lowering material quality.

If those interruptions are affecting production, would you be open to a short call to work out whether a pilot would be useful?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Christine,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I came across the accounts of automated buffing and robotic wheel painting at Ingersoll. We’re looking for one automated stage where we can quantify recovery time and test whether software reduces it without affecting quality. That would give us a defined starting point before trying anything broader.

Does that sound relevant to the operation? I’d be interested in a short call with the technical owner to see whether there’s a useful pilot here.

Best,
Andrew

after.subject: Ingersoll automation
after.body:
Hi Bruce,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the automated buffing and robotic wheel painting at Ingersoll. A retreading pilot could separate routine casing work from time lost recovering automated equipment, then test software against the interruptions that delay retread production. Casing quality would remain part of the comparison.

Would you be the right person for a short call about this, or could you point me toward whoever owns the process?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Brantford crumb rubber automation
contacts.body:
Hi Mike,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the ambient and cryogenic crumb-rubber processes at Brantford. A pilot could identify which interruptions account for the most lost production time on one grinding route, benchmark how they are recovered, and test software against those cases without compromising crumb quality.

Does your remit include Brantford? If this is a meaningful issue there, would you be open to a short call about a possible pilot, or could you point me toward the right person?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Barry,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the ambient and cryogenic crumb-rubber processes at Brantford. We’re looking for a crumb-rubber process where we can measure recovery burden and evaluate a software improvement on one route first. If it works at Brantford, we could then see whether the same approach makes sense at other CRM plants.

Would you be the right person for a short call about a Brantford pilot, or could you point me toward whoever currently owns the operation?

Best,
Andrew

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Kingston magnet recovery automation
contacts.body:
Hi Matthew,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the Kingston magnet-isolation pilot described as Mag-Xtract and later MagCycle. If that pilot remains active and the separation-cycle records are available, we could use them to isolate unplanned stops, reconstruct the recovery steps, and evaluate software against the cases taking the most operator time.

If there are recurring recovery cases worth reducing, would you be open to a short call to scope a useful starting point?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Joliette automation
contacts.body:
Hi Alain,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I came across the Machinex description of the optical sorting line at the Joliette centre. A sorting-line pilot could quantify productive time lost to clearing and restarting equipment, identify the recovery cases taking the most time, and test software against them while checking sorted-material output and quality.

If that is a meaningful issue at Joliette, would you be open to a short call, or could you point me toward the person responsible for that line?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Joliette automation
contacts.body:
Hi Yves,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I came across the Machinex description of the optical sorting line at the Joliette centre. If sorter and conveyor alarms are already logged, we could match them to the steps people take to get the line running again, identify the recurring stop-and-restart sequences, and test whether software can shorten them.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Hawkesbury automation
contacts.body:
Hi David,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the Hawkesbury updates on the milling line and double-batch runs. As Hawkesbury ramps up, we could establish which interruptions delay stable batch processing and evaluate software against those recovery cases. The useful result would be a measured change in the time people spend recovering the process, with completed runs and product quality checked alongside it.

Would you be open to a short call to see whether this addresses a real operating problem and which line would be a useful starting point?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Mukul,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the electronics-processing and plastics-shredding operation on Bren Road. If the shredder and line-stop records are available, we could use them to connect interruptions with the checks and resets needed to restart, rank the recurring recovery cases, and test whether software can reduce the time they consume.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Anna,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the electronics-processing and plastics-shredding operation on Bren Road. contacts.name: Ricky Morin

contacts.subject: Lethbridge automation
contacts.body:
Hi Ricky,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the rigid-plastics recovery and compounding operation in Lethbridge. We’re looking for an initial recycling pilot where we can measure how much productive time is being lost to recurring interventions, identify the recovery cases that matter most, and then see how much of that can be reduced in software without affecting output or resin quality.

If that is a meaningful problem at Lethbridge, would you be open to a short call about the line?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Martin,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the rigid-plastics recovery and compounding operation in Lethbridge. Lethbridge could offer a defined starting point for a pilot that quantifies recovery time and tests software against recurring processing interruptions. We’d track recovery time alongside output and resin quality before deciding whether the approach is worth trying at other plants.

If that is a meaningful issue at the facility, would you have 20 minutes to discuss a possible starting point with the relevant technical owner?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Trevor,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The connection between plastics recovery and compounding at Listowel caught my attention. We could measure the production time lost between an interruption and stable, in-spec output, identify the recovery cases contributing most, and evaluate whether software can reduce that gap at Listowel.

If recovery is costing the line meaningful productive time, would you have 20 minutes to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Surrey automation
contacts.body:
Hi Brad,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I came across the flexible-packaging sorting study carried out at the Surrey MRF. A pilot on the current flexible-packaging line could separate normal manual sorting from productive time lost recovering automation, then test whether software can reduce the latter without affecting separation quality.

Does that sound like an operating problem worth addressing? If so, would you be open to a 20-minute call to see whether a pilot is worth scoping?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.name: William Clark
contacts.reason: Likely owner or route to operating interruptions, operator recovery and a plant visit. Apollo location: Brantford, Ontario, Canada. Exact facility remit is not independently confirmed.
contacts.subject: Brantford tire automation
contacts.body:
Hi William,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the tire-shredding and crumb-rubber operation in Brantford. We’re looking for an initial recycling pilot where we can use any line data already being recorded to identify which interruptions are costing the most productive time, benchmark how they’re currently recovered, and then test whether some of those recoveries can be handled in software.

If that is a real issue on the Brantford line, would you be open to a short call to see whether there’s a useful pilot there?

Best,
Andrew
