Hi Shane,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the tire-shredding and crumb-rubber operation in Brantford. We could connect available shredder and conveyor events with the checks, clearances and resets around a stop, identify recurring recovery sequences, and evaluate which parts software could shorten without changing the required safety checks.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

before.subject: Brantford tires automation
before.body:
Hi Shane,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the tire-shredding and crumb-rubber operation in Brantford. We could connect available shredder and conveyor events with the checks, clearances and resets around a stop, identify recurring recovery sequences, and evaluate which parts software could shorten without changing the required safety checks.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Stephanie,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the extrusion work at Bromont and the production and quality checks operators make. A pilot could connect available extrusion records with the lab’s quality checks, identify what delays a return to in-spec material after an interruption, and test whether software can shorten that recovery without weakening the quality checks.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Junior,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I came across the optical-sorting work at Thetford Mines and the later expansion. With the expanded sorting operation, a pilot could identify which interventions cost the line the most productive time and test recovery software against them, checking material throughput and sorting quality alongside the result.

If recovery is costing the line meaningful productive time, would you have 20 minutes to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

Best,
Andrew

contacts.name: Ian Lorentz
contacts.reason: Quebec regional technical operations remit; Montreal-Est plant assignment still requires confirmation.
contacts.subject: Montréal-Est automation
contacts.body:
Hi Ian,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The optical sorting and mechanical separation at the Montréal-Est MRF caught my attention. A pilot could identify which interruptions across those stages consume the most productive time, benchmark how the line is recovered, and test software against the cases costing the most time without reducing sorting output or quality.

If those recoveries are taking meaningful time at Montréal-Est, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.reason: Likely owner or route to operating interruptions, operator recovery and a plant visit. Apollo location: Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Exact facility remit is not independently confirmed.
contacts.subject: Arrow Road automation
contacts.body:
Hi Todd,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the optical sorting and robots across the Arrow Road recycling facilities. A useful pilot would start with one line in one building, measure productive time lost to recovery, and test software against recurring interruptions. Keeping that scope fixed would let us compare output and material quality meaningfully.

If those interruptions are affecting production, would you be open to a short call to work out whether a pilot would be useful?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.name: Amit Parekh
contacts.reason: Likely owner or useful route to alarms, maintenance records and recovery work. Apollo location: Brantford, Ontario, Canada. Exact facility remit is not independently confirmed.
contacts.subject: Brantford automation
contacts.body:
Hi Amit,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The process of turning recovered plastics into waxes and additives at Brantford caught my attention. If the process-state records are available, we could use them to distinguish normal adjustments from unplanned recovery, identify the sequences that delay steady production, and evaluate software against repeatable cases within the process and product constraints.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Doug,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the Edmonton plant's use of robotics and automation alongside the plastics recycling operation. If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Amaranth automation
contacts.body:
Hi Kyle,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The combination of retreading, wheel refinishing and assembly at Amaranth caught my attention. We’re looking for an automated remanufacturing stage where a pilot can quantify recovery time and test whether software can reduce it. If there is an automated stage where recovery is taking meaningful time, we could start there and measure the result before trying anything broader.

Does that sound relevant to the operation? I’d be interested in a short call with the technical owner to see whether there’s a useful pilot here.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Anjou automation
contacts.body:
Hi Danick,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The connection between sorting, contaminant removal and compounding at Anjou caught my attention. If events from those stages are being recorded, we could connect them with the checks and adjustments needed to recover production, identify repeatable sequences, and evaluate software against the cases that delay in-spec output.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

before.subject: Anjou automation
before.body:
Hi Bruno,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

The connection between sorting, contaminant removal and compounding at Anjou caught my attention. A pilot could separate routine responses to incoming material from interruptions that cost useful production time, then test recovery software against the largest cases while checking resin output and quality.

If that is a material issue for the operation, would you be open to a short call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.name: Philippe Cote

contacts.subject: Saint-Étienne automation
contacts.body:
Hi Philippe,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the update on the completed sorting-line modernization at Saint-Étienne-des-Grès. Following the modernization, a useful pilot could establish which recovery tasks still cost the line productive time and test whether software can reduce that time while preserving material recovery and sorting quality.

If that is a material issue for the operation, would you be open to a short call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.name: Jens Dieckmann
contacts.reason: Likely owner or route to operating interruptions, operator recovery and a plant visit. Apollo location: Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Exact facility remit is not independently confirmed.
contacts.subject: Delta automation
contacts.body:
Hi Jens,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the project to expand polyethylene processing at Delta and improve recycled-polypropylene quality. A pilot could measure time lost returning an interrupted run to stable production, prioritize the recovery cases affecting usable plastic output, and evaluate software while tracking polyethylene and polypropylene quality alongside recovery time.

Does that sound like an operating problem worth addressing? Would you be open to a 20-minute call to see whether there’s a fit?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Mark,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I saw the project to expand polyethylene processing at Delta and improve recycled-polypropylene quality. We could connect available processing records with the adjustments and checks after an interruption, identify what delays a return to acceptable material quality, and test software against those repeatable recovery sequences.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Toronto plastics line automation
contacts.body:
Hi Ario,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the Toronto plastics recovery line announced in May, particularly the washing and density separation after shredding. If events from those stages are logged, we could connect them with operator interventions, trace which recovery sequences hold up the rest of the line, and evaluate whether software can shorten those cases while preserving recovered-plastic quality.

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Toronto plastics line automation
contacts.body:
Hi Rony,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I saw the Toronto plastics recovery line announced in May, particularly the washing and density separation after shredding. We could connect available shredder, washing and separation events with operator interventions, trace which recovery sequences hold up the rest of the line, and evaluate whether software can shorten those cases while preserving recovered-plastic quality.

If recovery is taking meaningful time on the line, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot?

Best,
Andrew

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

The combination of plastics sorting and resin production at Sarnia caught my attention. If events from those stages are being logged, we could connect them with operator recovery, identify sequences that require more than a single-machine restart, and test software against those cases while preserving resin specification.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Guilherme,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the infeed, hammermill and downstream separation at Richmond. A pilot could identify which interruptions in feeding, shredding or separation take the most productive time to recover, then test whether software can reduce that burden without compromising material output or safe operation.

If those recoveries are taking meaningful time at Richmond, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

before.subject: Richmond automation
before.body:
Hi Mark,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the infeed, hammermill and downstream separation at Richmond. We could scope one part of the Richmond line, establish the recovery burden and evaluate software against a defined set of recurring interruptions. That would provide a measured operating result before considering any broader deployment.

If that is a meaningful issue at the facility, would you have 20 minutes to discuss a possible starting point with the relevant technical owner?

Best,
Andrew

If those interruptions are a real issue, would you have 20 minutes for a technical call to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

after.subject: Granby automation
after.body:
Hi Kurt,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

The way the Granby robots sort cartons and HDPE, with people recovering cartons downstream, caught my attention. At Granby, we could keep routine manual sorting separate from actual robot or line recovery, then baseline the time lost to those recoveries. We would then test whether recovery software produces a measurable reduction in that time.

If there is a recurring recovery problem worth addressing, would you be open to a 20-minute call about a scoped pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.body:
Hi Vincent,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the washing and filtration improvements at Yamachiche. We could connect available washing and filtration events with operator adjustments, distinguish routine process work from recovery, and test software against sequences that delay a return to consistent output of recovered plastic.

Does that sound relevant to the line? I’d be glad to set up a 20-minute technical call to see whether we could make a useful difference.

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Sainte-Catherine automation
contacts.body:
Hi Stephane,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I came across the commissioning work on the polypropylene recovery line at Sainte-Catherine. A pilot on the recovery line could quantify productive time lost to recurring interruptions and test whether software can reduce it, with recovered-polypropylene output and quality included in the comparison.

If those interruptions are taking meaningful time at Sainte-Catherine, would you be open to a 20-minute technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Gatineau automation
contacts.body:
Hi David,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw that the Tricentris modernization includes replacing the older optical sorters at Gatineau. Depending on the replacement stage, we could baseline recovery on the current equipment, connect any available fault records with maintenance interventions, and test software against recurring cases. That would keep equipment changes separate from any software effect.

If this is relevant to Gatineau, would you be open to a short technical call, or could you point me toward the team responsible for that line?

Best,
Andrew

Hi David,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw the Lachute modernization plans, including the optical sorting and sorting robot. If that equipment is now in operation, we could connect any available sorter and robot event records with the maintenance recovery steps, identify repeatable sequences, and evaluate software against the cases taking the most time.

If this is relevant to Lachute, would you be open to a short technical call, or could you point me toward the team responsible for that line?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Terrebonne automation
contacts.body:
Hi David,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I saw that Terrebonne is part of the Tricentris optical-sorting modernization. We could connect any available optical-sorter and line event records with the maintenance recovery steps, establish which sequences recur, and evaluate software once the equipment configuration is stable enough to separate its effect from the replacement itself.

If this is relevant to Terrebonne, would you be open to a short technical call, or could you point me toward the team responsible for that line?

Best,
Andrew

contacts.subject: Rivière-du-Loup automation
contacts.body:
Hi Christian,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time lost when someone has to step in and recover an automated system.

I was reading about the Machinex optical and mechanical sorting line at Rivière-du-Loup. We could connect any logged optical and mechanical separation events with the steps needed to recover the line, identify recurring interruptions, and evaluate software against the recovery cases taking the most time.

If there are recurring recovery cases worth reducing, would you be open to a short call to scope a useful starting point?

Best,
Andrew

Hi Mauro,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the Machinex optical and mechanical sorting line at Rivière-du-Loup. A pilot could measure productive time lost to sorting and separation recovery, identify the recurring cases taking the most time, and test whether software reduces that burden without affecting the amount or quality of material recovered.

If recovery is costing the line meaningful productive time, would you have 20 minutes to see whether there’s a useful pilot here?

Best,
Andrew

before.subject: Rivière-du-Loup automation
before.body:
Hi Edmond,

I’m a UofT student building Wapahki, software for reducing the time automated systems lose when someone has to step in and recover them.

I was reading about the Machinex optical and mechanical sorting line at Rivière-du-Loup. We could connect available optical and mechanical separation events with the steps needed to recover the line, identify recurring interruptions, and evaluate software against the recovery cases taking the most time.

If that recovery work is taking meaningful time, would you be open to a short technical call about a possible pilot?

Best,
Andrew

queue.subject: Leak alerts when measurements arrive late
queue.body:
Hi Amir,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

A lot of my current work is about working out what happened from an incomplete picture of a system. With TaKaDu's network-event detection, I'd be curious when a missing pressure reading makes a leak harder to recognise, and when the surrounding measurements still give you enough information.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project around that question. One idea would be to replay network measurements with selected delays and compare how the event detection changes. Would that be useful to the team, or is there another detection or evaluation problem you'd rather have someone work on? I'd be doing it alongside my current co-op.

Happy to send my resume over, and happy to talk if it sounds worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

queue.subject: Battery schedules as flexibility prices change
queue.body:
Hi Archy,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The planning work has made me interested in decisions where the best action now depends on what you expect to need later. I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

The planning work has made me interested in routes where you can't finish every useful task in the time available. With TerraClear's rock maps, I'd be curious how the route should change when the goal is to remove the most troublesome rocks before the field is needed, rather than visit every mapped location.

I'd be interested in a small contract project comparing routes under the same operating window and seeing which rock-removal priorities each can cover. I could build the simulation alongside my current work, though I'd rather start with a planning question the team actually needs answered. Is that something worth a conversation?

Happy to send my resume over, and happy to talk if it sounds worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew
queue.decision: Weekly draft calendar only; fresh mailbox review required before any external action.

entries.name: Vibhor Sood
entries.last_sent_body:
Hi Vibhor,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

Burro seemed like a good fit because an outdoor robot needs to handle changing surroundings without someone constantly getting it unstuck. That connection between navigation and recovery is close to what I’ve been working on.

I was wondering if there might be a small contract project I could take ownership of alongside my current work. One thought was a simulation and evaluation harness around navigation recovery, testing what happens when a path becomes blocked or the robot is uncertain about its position, but I’d much rather work on whatever problem would actually be useful to the team.

I attached my resume for context; happy to jump on a quick call if there might be something worth exploring.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I’d like to apply that simulation work to problems where the answer changes while you’re still collecting the data, which is what interested me in Floodbase. When observations of a flood arrive at different times, I’d be curious how you separate the effect of a missing observation from the flood itself changing.

I was wondering whether there might be a project I could take ownership of alongside my current work, testing how delayed, missing or conflicting observations affect flood estimates. I’d be interested to hear whether that question is useful to the team or whether there’s something else you’d rather have someone work through.

Andrew

entries.last_sent_subject: Solar forecasts when cloud images are missing
entries.last_sent_body:
Hi Dan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I also emailed Peter earlier today, but wanted to reach out to you too as one of OCF's founders. I was reading about the solar forecasting work and got interested in how the model holds up when cloud imagery is missing; losing an observation just before cloud cover changes could make the next shift in solar generation much harder to predict.

That problem is close to work I'm already doing, and lately I've been looking for ways to apply more of my simulation and ML work to problems with a real-world benefit.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to replay forecasts with selected cloud images withheld and see which gaps cause the biggest errors in predicted solar generation, but if there’s another forecasting problem the team thinks would matter more in practice, I’d be happy to work on that as well.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew
